'''Meemann Chang''' ({{lang-zh|s=张弥曼}}; born 17 April 1936), also known as '''Zhang Miman''', is a Chinese [[Paleontology|paleontologist]] at the [[Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology|Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP)]]. She completed her undergraduate studies at [[Moscow University]] and completed her PhD thesis entitled 'The braincase of ''[[Youngolepis]]'', a Lower Devonian [[crossopterygian]] from Yunnan, south-western China' at [[Stockholm University]].<ref name="english.ivpp.cas.cn">{{cite web|url=http://english.ivpp.cas.cn/ns/es/201105/t20110513_69779.html|title=IVPP's Professor to Receive Honorary Degree from Chicago University----Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences|publisher=english.ivpp.cas.cn|accessdate=13 August 2015}}</ref> She was the first woman to become head of [[Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology|IVPP]] in 1983.<ref name="Rex">{{Cite journal | last1 = Dalton | first1 = R. | title = Palaeontology: Hooked on fossils | doi = 10.1038/439262a | journal = Nature | volume = 439 | issue = 7074 | pages = 262–263 | year = 2006 | pmid =  16421540| bibcode = 2006Natur.439..262D | s2cid = 4357313 | doi-access = free }}</ref> For her many career achievements, she received an honorary degree from the University of Chicago in 2011<ref name="english.ivpp.cas.cn"/> and the Romer-Simpson Medal from the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology in 2016.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://vertpaleo.org/past-award-winners-and-grant-recipients/|title=Past Award Winners And Grant Recipients|publisher=Society of Vertebrate Paleontology|accessdate=19 November 2023}}</ref>

==Biography==
Zhang was born into a wealthy and highly educated family in [[Nanjing]], [[Jiangsu]], on 17 April 1936, while her [[Ancestral home (Chinese)|ancestral home]] is in [[Shengzhou]], [[Zhejiang]].<ref name="watermelon">{{cite news|author1=Fu Yao ({{lang|zh|符遥}})|url=http://www.stdaily.com/index/fangtan/2018-04/16/content_659802.shtml |script-title=zh:杰出女科学家张弥曼：82岁成“国民女神” |work=stdaily.com |date=16 April 2018 |access-date=6 July 2021 |language=zh}}</ref> Her father graduated from the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name="watermelon"/> As a child, she was determined to become a doctor.<ref name="watermelon"/> After the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]] broke out, her family fled to different cities to take refuge. After initially living in [[Beibei District|Beibei]], [[Sichuan]], they then moved to [[Jiangxi]], and finally they settled in [[Nantong]].<ref name="watermelon"/>

After graduating from Shanghai Tongji High School in 1953, she was admitted to Beijing Institute of Geology (now [[China University of Geosciences (Beijing)]]). Soon after, she was sent to [[Moscow State University]] to study at the expense of the government. When she returned to China, she was dispatched to the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology of the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="watermelon"/> In 1965, she became a visiting scholar at the National Museum of Natural Science in [[Sweden]]. After the [[reform and opening up]] in 1980, she went to Sweden again and received her PhD from [[Stockholm University]] in 1982. She was director of the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in 1983 and held that office until 1990. She became chairman of the Paleontological Society of China in 1993, and served until 1997.

In 2011, she was awarded an honorary doctor of science degree from the University of Chicago.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.sciencenet.cn/htmlnews/2011/5/247131.shtm |script-title=zh:张弥曼院士被授予芝加哥大学荣誉科学博士学位 |work=sciencenet.cn |date=24 May 2011 |access-date=6 July 2021 |language=zh}}</ref> On 5 October 2015, she received an honorary doctoral degree from the Richard Gilder Graduate School of the [[American Museum of Natural History]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://casad.cas.cn/ysdt/201510/t20151013_4681844.html |script-title=zh:张弥曼院士荣获美国自然历史博物馆研究生院荣誉博士学位 |work=cas.cn |date=13 October 2015 |access-date=6 July 2021 |language=zh}}</ref> On 2 July 2021, [[List of minor planets: 347001–348000#347301–347400|asteroid 347336]] was named after her.<ref>{{cite news|author1=Wu Xiaodong ({{lang|zh|武晓东}})|url=https://news.sina.com.cn/c/2021-07-03/doc-ikqciyzk3343368.shtml |script-title=zh:太空又多了一颗中国星：“张弥曼星”！ |work=sina |date=3 July 2021 |access-date=4 July 2021 |language=zh}}</ref>

==Contributions==
Species named  in her honour include the extinct [[sarcopterygian]] fish ''[[Meemannia]]'',<ref name="Nature2006">{{Cite journal | last1 = Zhu | first1 = M. | last2 = Yu | first2 = X. | last3 = Wang | first3 = W. | last4 = Zhao | first4 = W. | last5 = Jia | first5 = L. | title = A primitive fish provides key characters bearing on deep osteichthyan phylogeny | doi = 10.1038/nature04563 | journal = Nature | volume = 441 | issue = 7089 | pages = 77–80 | year = 2006 | pmid =  16672968| bibcode = 2006Natur.441...77Z | s2cid = 1840338 }}</ref> the [[theropod]] dinosaur [[Sinovenator|''Sinovenator changii'']],<ref name="Nature2002">{{Cite journal | last1 = Xu | first1 = X. | last2 = Norell | first2 = M. A. | last3 = Wang | first3 = X. L. | last4 = Makovicky | first4 = P. J. | last5 = Wu | first5 = X. C. | title = A basal troodontid from the Early Cretaceous of China | doi = 10.1038/415780a | journal = Nature | volume = 415 | issue = 6873 | pages = 780–784 | year = 2002 | pmid =  11845206| bibcode = 2002Natur.415..780X | s2cid = 4417515 }}</ref> and the extinct [[Euornithes|ornithuromorph]] birds ''[[Archaeornithura|Archaeornithura meemannae]]''<ref name=Science>{{cite web|title=Feathered fossils from China reveal dawn of modern birds |author=Balter, Michael |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/feathered-fossils-china-reveal-dawn-modern-birds |date=5 May 2015 |accessdate=6 May 2015| work=Science}}</ref> and ''[[Meemannavis|Meemannavis ductrix]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=O' Connor JK, Stidham TA, Harris JD, Lamanna MC, Bailleul AM, Hu H, Wang M, You H|year=2021|title=Avian skulls represent a diverse ornithuromorph fauna from the Lower Cretaceous Xiagou Formation, Gansu Province, China|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jse.12823|journal=Journal of Systematics and Evolution|volume=60 |issue=5 |pages=1172–1198 |doi=10.1111/jse.12823|s2cid=245586113|url-access=subscription}}</ref> There is also a unique organ of yunnanolepid [[Antiarchi|antiarch]] [[Placodermi|placoderms]] named "Chang's Apparatus" after her.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Zhu|first=Min|date=1996|title=The phylogeny of the Antiarcha (Placodermi, Pisces), with the description of Early Devonian antiarchs from Qujing, Yunnan, China|url=https://www.academia.edu/download/24919671/Zhu1996b.pdf|journal=Bulletin du Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle|volume=18|page=243|quote=The opening of the CHANG's apparatus (a name erected here after Prof. M.-M. CHANG)}}{{dead link|date=July 2022|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

{{Citation | title = Morphology, Phylogeny and Paleobiogeography of Fossil Fishes | isbn = 978-3-89937-122-2 | last1 = Elliott | first1 = David K. | last2 = Maisey | first2 = John G. | last3 = Yu | first3 = Xiaobo |last4 = Miao | first4 = Desui | year = 2010 | publisher = Verlag Dr. Friedrich Pfeil | location = Munich}}, a special book volume on fossil fish, was published in her honour.

Chang notably first described<ref name="google">{{cite book|title=On Late Mesozoic fossil fishes from Zhejiang province, China|author1=Chang, M.|author2=Chou, C.|date=1977|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OL2HmQEACAAJ|accessdate=13 August 2015}}</ref> and later re-described<ref name="Redescription">{{Cite journal | last1 = Xu | first1 = G. H. I. | last2 = Chang | first2 = M. E. M. | doi = 10.1111/j.1096-3642.2009.00532.x | title = Redescription of †Paralycoptera wuiChang & Chou, 1977 (Teleostei: Osteoglossoidei) from the Early Cretaceous of eastern China | journal = Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society | volume = 157 | pages = 83–106 | year = 2009 | doi-access = free }}</ref> the fossil genus ''[[Paralycoptera]]'', and also described the fossil genera ''[[Diabolepis]]''<ref>Chang, M. & Yu, X. Structure and Phylogenetic significance of ''Diabolichthys speratus'' gen. et sp. nov.; a new Dipnoan-like from the lower Devonian of E. Yunnan; China. Journal of the Linnean Society of New South Wales, Sydney (1984)</ref> and ''[[Youngolepis]]''.<ref>Chang, M. & Yu, X. B. (1981) A new crossopterygian, Youngolepis praecursor, gen. et sp. nov., from the Lower Devonian of Eastern Yunnan, China. Scientia Sinica 24:89-97.</ref>

==Honours==
* 1991 Member of the [[Chinese Academy of Engineering]]
* 1995 Foreign Fellow of the [[Linnean Society of London]] 
* 2011 Foreign Fellow of the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]]
* 2015 Doctor of Science, Honoris Causa [Richard Gilder Graduate School of the American Museum of Natural History]
* 2016 [[Romer-Simpson Medal]], [[Society of Vertebrate Paleontology]]
* 2018 and 2019 [[Asian Scientist 100]], ''[[Asian Scientist]]''

==Awards==
On November 13, 2017, Chang was awarded the [[L'Oréal-UNESCO Awards for Women in Science]]. She was nominated for "her pioneering work on fossil records leading to insights on how aquatic vertebrates adapted to life and land."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://english.cqnews.net/html/2018-03/09/content_43952371.htm |title=Chinese scientist named 2018 L'Oreal-UNESCO Women in Science laureate |newspaper=cqnews.net |date=2018-03-09 }}</ref> In November 2017, Chang was also awarded the [[Ho Leung Ho Lee Foundation|Ho Leung Ho Lee Foundation Achievement Prize]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-03-08|title=26 Fantastic Female Scientists|url=https://www.asianscientist.com/2019/03/features/26-fantastic-female-scientists/|access-date=2020-10-13|website=Asian Scientist Magazine|language=en-US}}</ref>
